children.author: walrus01
children.text:
I very recently spent a lot of time using deepseek v4 flash 0731 before it was superseded by newer more capable things (glm 5.3-flash, v4.1 flash 1017, etc) and I am exceedingly skeptical of anyone that claims to get good QUALITY results out of it at that size. Whatever they're doing to shrink it will make it worse than an unsloth Q2XS quantization of it or equivalent. That size of model needs something like 150GB of RAM to run properly with full unquantized kv cache and not with a ton of training data discarded.

I remain exceedingly skeptical of people who are claiming to run fairly large models in ridiculously tiny sizes. For comparison a 'regular' version of v4 flash 0731 has file sizes more like this: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF

Even the 97GB Q2XS will show very significant divergence from the full precision thing. Running a lobotomized model just to say you're doing it is really not accomplishing anything special.

children.author: bitexploder
children.text: And things like GSQ-RCO optimization from ISTA labs, EXL that you linked. Preserving bits for certain (large) domains like agentic coding. Pruning others. It really works and creates functional models.

I think your leading statement is a bit more authoritative than what the linked paper actually demonstrates. It demonstrates your claimed qualities for specific algorithms, methodologies, and models.

It explicitly says that Quantization-Aware Training is out of scope, may reveal different trends and has potential for extreme quantization. Heavily-quantized model releases today generally use QAT or something similar, so I don't think the paper can be universally applied to modern quants (e.g. [0]).

That said, I don't see any evidence that TFA does any of that so the paper's claims may be quite applicable there.

[0]: https://huggingface.co/vcruz305/DSV4.1-Flash-1017-SAGE-REXL3...

Something to keep in mind with aggressive quantisation, is that it's been empirically proven [1] that (1) quantisation has non-linear performance behaviour, and (2) generally the peak size-to-performance ratio occurs at 4-bit; anything lower and you will see significant reduction in performance.

Also, I've been playing with speech models for the past 2 years, and for me anything below 8-bit is a huge drop in quality; so quantisation for LLMs and for other bespoke modality models, is not 1:1.

[1] "Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models", TUM, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.10855

Interesting. There are quite a few forks of llama.cpp where streaming weights has been successful, or special quants / decompressing before processing.

- Bonsai Qwen 3.8 27B

- Strata

- Pulsar

- This...

I just wish upstream Llama.cpp would accept the PRs faster - they build multiple times per day, but their PR backlog was 1.7K last I checked, which is a ridiculously impractical number to review with a few volunteers.

I watched the Qwen 3.8 Bonsai feature and it took over 3 weeks from creation to be reviewed, and even then it doesn't include the patches for bugs, that they fixed downstream and simply gave up pushing to upstream because the process was so laborious.

So they end up with delayed or missing model support, and half working implementations like Bonsai's Hadamard Folding, and new models lose out on this kind of optimisation.

I suppose this is fine if you intend your project to be the reference project for forks and encourage this kind of specialisation, but I don't think that's intentional.

At least I can use llamaswap to juggle the inference engines and models on the fly, and abstract the fact I need to install 3 or 4 different ones.
